statement: Children under the age of fifteen should not be allowed to own a smartphone.
question: To what extent do you agree or disagree?
model:
Few parental decisions now generate as much anxiety as the question of when to hand a child a smartphone. Some argue that the devices should be withheld entirely until the mid-teens. Although I sympathise with the concern behind this view, I disagree with an outright ban, since careful, gradual access is both more realistic and more educational.

It is certainly true that smartphones pose genuine risks to young people. Social media platforms are deliberately engineered to hold attention, and a twelve-year-old has far less capacity than an adult to resist the pull of endless notifications. Teachers frequently report pupils arriving at school exhausted after scrolling late into the night, and there is mounting evidence linking heavy use to anxiety and low self-esteem, particularly among girls who compare themselves with edited images of their peers.

Nevertheless, prohibition tends to postpone problems rather than solve them. A teenager who receives a phone on their fifteenth birthday, with no previous experience, is arguably more vulnerable than one who has learnt over several years how to recognise scams, manage screen time and handle unkind messages. Moreover, a phone is no longer a mere toy; it is how many families coordinate journeys, how schools share homework and how children stay in touch with a parent who works abroad.

A more sensible approach, in my view, is to treat smartphone ownership as a privilege that expands with maturity. A ten-year-old might have a basic phone for calls and maps, with social media introduced later and under supervision. Parents can also model restraint themselves, since children quickly notice when adults preach moderation while checking their own screens at the dinner table.

In conclusion, the dangers of early smartphone use are real, but a blanket ban is too blunt an instrument. Guided, incremental access offers a far better preparation for a world in which these devices are unavoidable.
